From Retrieved Context to Runtime Control: Adaptive Compression for Edge-based RAG
Zlatan Feric and Amir Taherin contributed equally.
Proceedings of the ACM AI Leadership Summit

Argues that the context-compression ratio in edge retrieval-augmented generation is a first-class runtime control knob: because the compressor runs on the same SoC as the generator, what matters is the net benefit after compressor overhead, and the optimal ratio shifts with workload and system state — motivating online, workload-aware control.
Also presented as a poster in the Future Leaders of AI program at the ACM AI Leadership Summit 2026.
ALBIREO: Adaptive, Energy-Efficient Inference Framework for Video Object Detection on the Edge

A detector-agnostic, training-free framework that decides at runtime which video frames actually require detector inference, bridging the rest with lightweight motion prediction, cutting energy per frame substantially while preserving — and in some scenes improving — detection accuracy on edge GPUs.
Examining Failures and Repairs on Supercomputers with Multi-GPU Compute Nodes
IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

Analyzes multi-year failure and repair logs from GPU-accelerated supercomputers with multi-GPU compute nodes, characterizing how GPU, node, and interconnect failures evolve across system generations and how large-scale systems recover in practice.
Energy-Efficient 360-Degree Video Rendering on FPGA via Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design
ACM/SIGDA International Symposium on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays

Co-designs the 360° video rendering algorithm with an FPGA architecture, restructuring the processing pipeline to fit on-chip memory budgets and deliver energy-efficient real-time rendering on a Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC.
RAGMark: A Comprehensive Framework for Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
IEEE International Symposium on Workload Characterization

A modular benchmarking framework for retrieval-augmented generation that attributes latency, energy, GPU utilization, memory behavior, and answer quality to individual pipeline stages, and uses that attribution to characterize how retrieval depth, reranking, and context compression shift bottlenecks and interact across stages.
Hydra: Phase-Aware Workload Characterization of LLM Inference across Edge SoC Generations, Backends, and Quantization Levels

Phase-aware measurement methodology and characterization of large-language-model inference across three generations of NVIDIA edge SoCs (Xavier, Orin, Thor), two inference backends, and multiple quantization formats, attributing latency, power, energy, and memory behavior to prefill and decode phases across a large per-prompt measurement corpus.
Stretch: Exploiting Service Level Degradation for Energy Management in Mixed-Criticality Systems
CSI Symposium on Real-Time and Embedded Systems and Technologies

Introduces Stretch, an energy-management technique for mixed-criticality real-time systems that trades controlled service-level degradation of low-criticality tasks for energy savings under reliability constraints.
Reliability-Aware Energy Management in Mixed-Criticality Systems

A reliability-aware energy-management framework for mixed-criticality embedded systems that exploits slack and controlled service degradation of low-criticality workloads to save energy while preserving reliability guarantees for safety-critical tasks.
Cross-Platform Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models from Edge to Cloud GPUs

Characterizes how vision-language-action models scale across the hardware spectrum — from Jetson-class edge SoCs to datacenter GPUs — profiling latency, throughput, and memory behavior to identify where each platform class becomes the right deployment target for robotic policies.
VOTE: Vision-Language-Action Optimization with Trajectory Ensemble Voting

An optimization approach for vision-language-action models that ensembles candidate action trajectories through voting, improving robotic policy efficiency; evaluated with deployments spanning edge and datacenter GPUs.
Human Cognition in Machines: A Unified Perspective of World Models
Timothy Rupprecht, Pu Zhao, Amir Taherin, Arash Akbari, Arman Akbari, Yumei He, and Tooba Imtiaz contributed equally to this research.

A survey that organizes world-model research by the cognitive functions each line of work innovates — memory, perception, language, reasoning, imagining, motivation, and metacognition — presents a unified conceptual framework spanning all seven, identifies motivation and metacognition as under-researched, and introduces epistemic world models for scientific-discovery agents operating over structured knowledge.
Detector-agnostic, training-free adaptive inference for video object detection on edge GPUs

Roughly one in five detector invocations can be skipped on driving video while accuracy is preserved — and in some settings slightly improved, because motion prediction bridges frames where the detector flickers.
On its flagship configuration, skipping cuts energy per frame by 17.6% and per-frame energy-delay product by 24.9% while AP@50 rises by 0.8 points.
The mechanism is detector-agnostic: across three detector families and two SoC generations, energy falls 12–18% with accuracy held within about one AP point — no retraining required.
The skip rate adapts naturally to scene dynamics: static scenes skip aggressively, high-motion scenes fall back to dense inference.

## Problem

Video object detection on the edge runs an expensive detector on every frame, even when
consecutive frames are nearly identical. On battery- and thermally-constrained platforms,
that uniform effort wastes energy exactly where it is scarcest — yet naive frame skipping
breaks accuracy the moment the scene changes.

## Central idea

Let uncertainty decide. ALBIREO tracks objects with a lightweight constant-acceleration
Kalman filter and invokes the real detector only when the tracker's confidence degrades —
so computation follows scene dynamics instead of the frame clock. Because the decision
logic sits outside the detector, the method is training-free and works unchanged across
detector architectures.

## Approach

Detected objects are propagated through a 10-dimensional Kalman state; covariance growth
triggers real inference. Rescue logic catches detector flicker (objects that momentarily
vanish from detector output), and a scene screen suppresses inference on empty roads.
Evaluated on BDD100K driving clips across YOLO11x, YOLO26x, and RF-DETR on two Jetson
generations, with full per-frame energy accounting — the adaptation overhead is charged
against the savings.

## Role

I lead the project end to end: the scheduling framework, the evaluation methodology, and
the cross-detector/cross-platform study.

Phase-aware characterization of LLM inference across three generations of edge SoCs
The joint choice of platform, backend, and precision spans a 1.8–2.4× range in energy per prompt — no single knob explains the gap.
A backend can win end-to-end while being slower per token: runtime structure (orchestration, de-tokenization) dominates latency, not kernel speed alone.
Power is not monotonic in bit-width: Q6_K draws more power and runs hotter than Q8_0 due to k-quant unpacking and scaling overheads.
Identical GPU-utilization readings mean different things across SoC generations because of DVFS behavior — raw utilization is not comparable without phase and clock context.
Deployability can be limited by allocator behavior rather than memory capacity: several F16 configurations fail on a 32 GB SoC because the software stack caps large contiguous allocations.

## Problem

Deploying a language model on an edge SoC means choosing a platform, an inference backend,
and a quantization level — and the consequences of those choices are entangled. Aggregate
metrics like tokens per second hide where time and energy actually go, and results measured
on one SoC generation do not transfer to the next.

## Central idea

Hydra attributes latency, power, energy, and memory behavior to the *phases* of LLM
inference — prefill and decode — under a common measurement schema applied identically
across hardware generations, backends, and precision formats. Phase-level attribution is
what makes cross-platform comparisons meaningful: the same aggregate throughput can come
from completely different phase behavior.

## Approach

We characterize 13 open models (1B–8B parameters) across two inference backends and
multiple quantization formats on three consecutive generations of NVIDIA edge SoCs
(Xavier, Orin, Thor), collecting synchronized per-prompt, per-phase records of latency,
power, energy, temperature, clocks, and memory traffic into a unified corpus of more than
one hundred thousand measurements.

## Role

I lead the project: measurement methodology, the cross-generation experimental campaign,
and the analysis, working with a multi-student team and our collaborators.

Stage-level benchmarking of retrieval-augmented generation: where latency, energy, and quality actually come from
RAG pipelines: retrieval, reranking, context compression, generation
Autoregressive generation dominates latency in naive RAG pipelines, but context-reduction techniques shift the bottleneck across compute, memory bandwidth, and preprocessing stages.
Reranking and compression compound: reranking shrinks the compressor’s own workload, and together they reduce prefill and KV-cache traversal costs — lowering energy consumption by up to 66%.
Cross-stage interactions are strong: small upstream context reductions cascade through downstream latency, memory traffic, and energy.
Stage-level attribution of energy, GPU utilization, and bandwidth — measured jointly with answer quality — exposes trade-offs that end-to-end metrics hide.

## Problem

A RAG pipeline is a chain of very different stages — retrieval, reranking, context
compression, generation — but it is usually measured as a single black box. That makes it
impossible to say *which* stage to optimize, or how a change upstream (retrieve fewer
passages, compress harder) propagates through the system downstream.

## Central idea

Benchmark the pipeline the way a systems person would profile a program: attribute
latency, energy, GPU utilization, memory behavior, and answer quality to each stage
individually, then sweep the configuration space — retrieval depth, model scale,
reranking, compression, vector-database placement — efficiently enough to map the
interactions between stages.

## Approach

RAGMark separates pipeline stages, timing, and resource monitoring into modular
components, and amortizes model and index loading across thousands of configurations so
large sweeps stay tractable. The stage-level attribution handles CUDA-asynchronous,
overlapping execution with synchronized stage boundaries and interval-sampled power
integrated over per-stage windows.

## Role

Joint work with Zlatan Feric, with our collaborators at Northeastern. The project also
seeds the adaptive-compression direction presented at the ACM AI Leadership Summit: once
stage-level costs are measurable, compression stops being a preprocessing step and becomes
a runtime control knob.

How vision-language-action models scale from power-constrained edge SoCs to datacenter GPUs
Architectural choices — action tokenization and backbone size — strongly influence throughput and memory footprint, independent of raw hardware capability.
Power-constrained edge devices degrade non-linearly, yet some edge configurations match or exceed older datacenter GPUs — challenging the assumption that robotic inference belongs in the datacenter.
High-throughput VLA variants are achievable without significant accuracy loss on the LIBERO benchmark.
Accuracy and system-level metrics (latency, throughput, peak memory) must be measured together: the deployment sweet spot moves with the power budget.

## Problem

Vision-language-action models are becoming the standard policy class for robotic control,
but how their performance scales across model architectures and hardware platforms — and
what power budgets that scaling implies — is poorly understood. Robots ship with edge
SoCs, while most VLA benchmarking happens on datacenter GPUs.

## Central idea

Evaluate representative VLA architectures *across the whole hardware spectrum* under
explicit power constraints, measuring task accuracy jointly with latency, throughput, and
peak memory — so that platform selection becomes an evidence-based decision rather than a
default to the biggest GPU available.

## Approach

Five representative VLA models — state-of-the-art baselines plus two newly proposed
architectures — are evaluated on the LIBERO benchmark across edge platforms under varying
power budgets and across high-performance datacenter GPU configurations, producing scaling
trends for both task and system metrics.

## Role

First author of the GLSVLSI 2026 paper; I led the cross-platform measurement study within
a larger VLA research effort that also produced the VOTE trajectory-ensemble optimization
(arXiv preprint, second author).
